A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors, and central research question. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data, binary-CIFAR, and ResNet experiments in Section 4, plus noisy-feature experiments in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original binary-CIFAR experiments and a shaded-MNIST background-shift experiment in Section 4, with results averaged over five training runs.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same ERM/weight-decay, label-smoothing, and Mixup training procedures and objectives. Architecture changes concern experimental testbeds; no new training method or modification to these procedures is proposed.

E1.justification: v2 retains the binary CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 class pairs but removes the synthetic classification task and full multiclass CIFAR experiments with appended class-specific channels. It adds ten-class shaded MNIST, with class-correlated background colors permuted between training and testing.

E2.justification: The comparisons continue to evaluate weight decay, label smoothing, and Mixup, with ordinary ERM represented by zero hyperparameter settings. Invariant risk minimization is newly cited to motivate the MNIST setup but is not evaluated as a comparator.

E3.justification: The multiclass evaluation changes from 100-epoch ResNet-18 training with fixed hyperparameters and epoch-wise error curves to a two-layer ReLU network with 2048 hidden units, 20 epochs, and full hyperparameter sweeps on shaded MNIST. These are replacement experiments under different conditions. The retained binary-CIFAR splits, preprocessing, optimizer settings, and sweeps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's Appendix B tests whether conclusions survive nonzero variance in spurious features, including a reported sensitivity of ResNet weight decay to Gaussian noise; these analyses disappear. v2 adds background-permutation robustness testing and nonlinear-model hyperparameter sensitivity on shaded MNIST. The binary-CIFAR weight-ratio diagnostic is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over five training runs and shaded one-standard-deviation bands. No change in repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing practices is documented.

E6.justification: The binary-CIFAR plots are identical: v1 Figures 2 and 3 become v2 Figures 1 and 2. Synthetic, ResNet, and noisy-feature results are removed. New shaded-MNIST results show roughly 10–15% test error with positive weight decay versus approximately 50–70% for label smoothing and Mixup (v2 Figure 3). These are new-condition results, not comparable-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 substantially revises the binary data assumptions and proofs, replacing exact zero-weight conclusions under zero conditional variance with variance-dependent bounds. The binary Mixup theorem adds a symmetry requirement on the mixing distribution. New multiclass Propositions 3.9 and 3.10 assert output-variance loss bounds, supported by a new Jensen-gap lemma and additional Appendix A proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list expand the formal claims beyond linear separable feature selection to loss bounds for general nonlinear, multiclass models. They also elevate failure under class-correlated background shifts across practical hyperparameters to a main contribution. The central warning that label augmentation can favor low-variance spurious features remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains why weak background intensities are needed for weight decay to succeed and explicitly limits its general-model theory to loss bounds without optimization-dynamics guarantees. It adds a small-scale-experiment limitation, while removing v1's discussion of noise-induced weight-decay failure and its possible dependence on experimental settings.

D1.justification: The documented experimental recipes substantially change: synthetic sampling, Gaussian channel concatenation, and uniform/Gaussian noise instructions are removed. v2 specifies shaded-MNIST background intensities, train/test color permutation, network width, and training duration. The PyTorch/P100 disclosure and retained binary-CIFAR implementation details remain unchanged; no code-access information is added.

R1.justification: Most related-work discussion is retained. v2 adds Arjovsky et al. (2020) to position the background-shift experiment and removes He et al. (2015) with the ResNet study. Its comparison with earlier Mixup feature-learning work now qualifies the mixing distributions as symmetric.

P1.justification: The contribution roadmap becomes a three-part contribution list, preliminaries are reorganized, and the data model moves into a split binary/multiclass theory section. Experimental explanations and appendix organization are substantially rewritten, and explicit Limitations and Broader Impacts paragraphs are added. The conclusion also corrects v1's reversal of which variance features are learned.

P2.justification: The synthetic plots, ResNet learning curves, channel-concatenation illustration, and appendix noise panels are removed. v2 adds a paired shaded-MNIST sample/performance figure. The retained binary-CIFAR figures are resized and repositioned with unchanged plotted content, substantially altering the presentation of the empirical evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 adds a useful background-shift sweep and clearer limitations, but removes the ResNet and nonzero-variance robustness evidence. Its central theoretical expansion is also not securely established: Appendix A.3 does not justify replacing conditional Jensen benchmarks with the global loss optima used in the new general-distribution bounds. Because this gap affects the main claimed gain, alongside mixed changes in empirical support, a reliable net-quality direction cannot be established.
